brief.situation: 09:20 on a medical unit. You go to give Mr. Brooke in bed 12 his ordered mealtime insulin lispro and find it already signed out at 09:05, by you. You realize you gave it to Mr. Brooks in bed 14.
handover: Mr. Brooks, bed 14, is 76, admitted with cellulitis, no diabetes. He ate about half his breakfast.
Mr. Brooke, bed 12, has type 2 diabetes and still has not had his mealtime insulin.

Unit policy: a medication error is reported at once to the provider and the charge nurse, the patient is assessed and treated, and an event report is filed; disclosure to the patient is planned with the provider and charge nurse. The unit's hypoglycemia protocol: 15 g fast carbohydrate for a conscious patient under 70 mg/dL, recheck in 15 minutes.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each assessment takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

source.note: Glucose falls as the lispro peaks in a patient without diabetes. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
It falls more slowly after oral carbohydrate. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

why.question: What do you do about the error, and why does reporting it now matter?

parts.label: Why now
parts.criteria: Rapid-acting insulin peaks within 30 to 90 minutes; a man without diabetes will become hypoglycemic; reporting now lets the provider order IV dextrose and monitoring before harm; reporting is every provider's responsibility.
parts.modelAnswer: The lispro will peak in the next hour, and he doesn't have diabetes, so his glucose will keep falling. If I report it now, the provider can order dextrose and checks before he has a seizure. Hiding it only delays that.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Checks his glucose and treats per protocol; calls the provider at once and tells the charge nurse; event report; honest documentation; bed 12's missed dose raised; disclosure to the patient planned with the provider and charge nurse.
parts.modelAnswer: Check his glucose and give juice per protocol, call the provider now and tell the charge nurse, and file the event report. Document honestly, flag that bed 12 missed his dose, and join the planned disclosure.

scoring.modelReasoning: Bed 12's rapid-acting insulin was given to Mr. Brooks, who has no diabetes, 15 minutes ago; it will peak within the next hour and his glucose will keep falling. Reporting now is what allows the provider to order IV dextrose and frequent checks before harm. Check his glucose, give 15 g of fast carbohydrate per protocol, call the provider at once and tell the charge nurse, file the event report, and document the facts honestly, including that bed 12 missed his dose. Disclosure to Mr. Brooks is planned with the provider and charge nurse. Waiting to see whether harm happens, or leaving the record wrong, turns an error into an injury.
